desc:
In one operation you choose two different indices i and j of nums and do nums[i] += 2 and nums[j] -= 2 (values may become any integer, including negative ones).

The array nums is said to match target when both contain the same values with the same multiplicities, in any order. Return the minimum number of operations needed to make nums match target. The input guarantees that this is possible.

nums = [8, 12, 6], target = [2, 14, 10]   -> 2
nums = [1, 2, 5],  target = [4, 1, 3]     -> 1
constraints: It is always possible to make nums match target
hints: An operation never changes the parity of any element, so even values can only turn into even values and odd values into odd values.
That splits the task into two independent ones: an even group and an odd group. Within one group, which element of nums should become which element of target?

Sort the even values of both arrays and pair them in order (same for the odd values). Sum the absolute differences of all pairs; every operation fixes at most 2 units on the 'too small' side and 2 units on the 'too large' side, so the answer is that sum divided by 4.
editorial: The parity argument fixes the two groups. Inside a group, the cheapest way to turn one multiset into another by moving values is to match the sorted lists position by position (the same exchange argument as for minimizing the sum of absolute differences of a matching).

Let D be the total amount by which elements must go up. Since the sums are equal, the total amount by which elements must go down is also D, and the sum of all absolute differences is 2D. One operation raises one element by 2 and lowers another by 2, so exactly D / 2 operations are needed and enough; this equals (sum of absolute differences) / 4. Sorting makes it O(n log n).
